modules.name: Sentinel Lymph Node Mapping (ICG) in Endometrial, Cervical & Vulvar Cancers

mustKnow.fact: Sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping utilizing near-infrared fluorescence imaging with Indocyanine Green (ICG, 1.25 mg/mL injected superficially and deeply at the 3 and 9 o'clock cervical positions) achieves bilateral mapping success rates exceeding 85% to 90% in endometrial and cervical cancers.
mustKnow.source: Rossi et al. Lancet Oncol 2017 (FIRES Trial)

mustKnow.fact: The FIRES prospective multi-center trial established that SLN mapping has a negative predictive value of 99.6% and sensitivity of 97.2% for detecting nodal metastases in clinical stage I endometrial cancer, confirming its safety as a replacement for full lymphadenectomy.

The standardized NCCN surgical SLN algorithm mandates: peritoneal evaluation, excision of all mapped green/fluorescent nodes, removal of any clinically suspicious or enlarged lymph nodes regardless of mapping, and mandatory side-specific systematic hemipelvic lymphadenectomy on any hemi-pelvis that fails to map.

Pathologic processing of SLNs requires protocol-directed ultrastaging: bisection of lymph node along long axis, serial sectioning at 50 to 250 um intervals, hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) staining, and anti-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) immunohistochemistry to detect low-volume metastases.

Nodal metastasis volume is categorized by AJCC/FIGO into three tiers: Macrometastases (>2.0 mm), Micrometastases (>0.2 mm to <=2.0 mm or >200 cells), and Isolated Tumor Cells (ITCs, single cells or small clusters <=0.2 mm and <=200 cells).

Isolated tumor cells (ITCs, pN0(i+)) in low-risk endometrial cancer do not adversely impact progression-free survival in retrospective cohort studies and many centers safely observe patients without adjuvant systemic chemotherapy.

In early cervical cancer (stage IA1 with LVSI through IB2), the prospective SENTICOL I and II trials demonstrated that bilateral SLN detection is oncologically safe, while avoiding the 30% risk of chronic lower extremity lymphedema associated with complete pelvic lymphadenectomy.
mustKnow.source: Lecuru et al. J Clin Oncol 2011

mustKnow.fact: Failure of bilateral mapping occurs in 10% to 15% of cases and is most commonly attributed to prior pelvic radiation, severe adhesions, marked obesity (BMI >40 kg/m2), anatomical vascular variants, or tumor blockage of lymphatic channels by macrometastatic emboli.

modules.name: Pelvic Exenteration: Anterior, Posterior, Total & Urinary Diversions

mustKnow.fact: Pelvic exenteration is an ultraradical surgical procedure designed with curative intent for central, isolated pelvic recurrence of cervical, vaginal, or vulvar carcinoma following prior definitive radiation therapy, in the complete absence of pelvic sidewall or distant metastatic disease.
Anterior pelvic exenteration comprises en bloc resection of uterus, cervix, vagina, bladder, and urethra with creation of a urinary conduit, sparing the rectum and anal sphincter.
Posterior pelvic exenteration comprises en bloc resection of uterus, cervix, vagina, rectum, and anal canal with permanent end-colostomy, sparing the bladder and lower urinary tract.

Total pelvic exenteration involves complete removal of all pelvic viscera (bladder, urethra, uterus, cervix, vagina, rectum, and anal canal) with concomitant creation of both a wet stoma (urinary diversion) and dry stoma (fecal colostomy).

Absolute contraindications to pelvic exenteration include extra-pelvic distant metastases, peritoneal carcinomatosis, tumor fixation to pelvic sidewall bone or sciatic nerve roots, bilateral hydronephrosis from sidewall tumor encasement, and poor functional performance status.

The standard incontinent urinary diversion is the Bricker ileal conduit: an isolated 15 to 20 cm segment of terminal ileum (taken 15 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve) mobilized with intact mesentery, bilateral spatulated ureteroileal anastomoses (Wallace or Bricker technique), and cutaneous stoma.

Continent urinary reservoirs (e.g., Miami pouch or Indiana pouch using detubularized right colon with plicated terminal ileum) provide continent catheterizable conduits with an antireflux mechanism, suitable in selected motivated patients with normal renal and hepatic function.

Pelvic dead space obliteration and pelvic floor reconstruction following exenteration requires pedicled myocutaneous flaps (vertical rectus abdominis myocutaneous [VRAM] flap or gracilis flap) or omental pedicle flap, which dramatically reduces pelvic floor herniation, pelvic sepsis, and fistula formation.

modules.name: Surgical Pelvic Neuroanatomy, Retroperitoneal Spaces & Vascular Control

topics.book: Berek & Hacker 7e Ch 23, DiSaia & Creasman 10e Ch 18

mustKnow.fact: The avascular paravesical space is bounded laterally by the external iliac vessels and obturator internus muscle, medially by the obliterated umbilical artery (superior vesical artery), posteriorly by the cardinal ligament (paracervix), and anteriorly by the pubic bone.

The avascular pararectal space is bounded medially by the rectum and uterosacral ligament, laterally by the internal iliac artery, posteriorly by the sacrum, and anteriorly by the cardinal ligament; the ureter runs along its medial leaf attached to the posterior peritoneum.

The cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt's ligament / lateral cervical ligament) separates the paravesical space anteriorly from the pararectal space posteriorly, transmitting the uterine artery which crosses superior and anterior to the ureter ('water under the bridge') approximately 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix.

The presacral (retrorectal) space lies between the parietal fascia covering the anterior sacrum and the visceral fascia of the rectum (fascia propria); dissection in this plane must avoid the presacral venous plexus (draining into middle sacral veins), which lacks valves and causes catastrophic hemorrhage if torn.

Ligation of the internal iliac (hypogastric) artery reduces pelvic pulse pressure by 85% and blood flow by 48%, achieving effective hemostasis for intractable pelvic hemorrhage via extensive collateral circulation (lumbar-iliolumbar, middle sacral-lateral sacral, superior rectal-middle rectal).

Internal iliac artery ligation is performed 3 to 4 cm distal to the common iliac bifurcation, carefully dissecting the artery off the underlying internal iliac vein and passing a right-angle clamp from lateral to medial to avoid vascular laceration.

The pelvic autonomic nervous system consists of the sympathetic hypogastric nerves (arising from superior hypogastric plexus at aortic bifurcation L5-S1) and the parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes, S2-S4), which coalesce to form the inferior hypogastric plexus lateral to the rectum.

The obturator nerve (arising from posterior lumbar plexus L2-L4) traverses the lateral pelvic sidewall deep to the external iliac vein, crossing the obturator internus muscle and exiting via the obturator canal; iatrogenic transection produces loss of thigh adduction and medial thigh sensory anesthesia.

modules.name: Recurrent Ovarian Cancer, Platinum Sensitivity & Secondary Cytoreduction (DESKTOPIII)

mustKnow.fact: Platinum-free interval (PFI) is the duration between completion of the last platinum chemotherapy and disease relapse, historically classifying recurrence into platinum-refractory (progression on therapy), platinum-resistant (PFI <6 months), partially platinum-sensitive (PFI 6-12 months), and fully platinum-sensitive (PFI >12 months).

The prospective randomized phase III DESKTOP III trial demonstrated that secondary cytoreductive surgery followed by chemotherapy in platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer significantly prolonged median overall survival (53.7 vs 46.0 months; HR 0.75) and progression-free survival strictly in patients who achieved complete resection (R0, median OS 61.9 vs 46.0 months).

The AGO score is a validated clinical selection tool for secondary cytoreduction: a positive score requires ECOG performance status 0, complete resection (R0) at primary surgery, and absence of gross ascites (<500 mL); a positive AGO score predicts an R0 complete debulking rate >75% at secondary surgery.

In contrast, the prospective GOG-213 trial evaluated secondary cytoreduction without mandatory preoperative AGO score selection criteria and showed no overall survival improvement for secondary surgery (median OS 50.6 vs 64.7 months; HR 1.29), highlighting the critical role of rigorous patient selection.
terms: no OS benefit in unselected cohort

mustKnow.fact: For platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer, standard re-induction chemotherapy regimens include carboplatin plus pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD), carboplatin plus gemcitabine, or carboplatin plus paclitaxel, with PLD preferred due to lower neurotoxicity and alopecia.
mustKnow.source: Pujade-Lauraine et al. J Clin Oncol 2010 (CALYPSO)

mustKnow.fact: The AURELIA phase III trial demonstrated that adding bevacizumab to single-agent chemotherapy (paclitaxel, topotecan, or pegylated liposomal doxorubicin) doubled median progression-free survival (6.7 vs 3.4 months; HR 0.48) and improved objective response rates in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.
mustKnow.source: Pujade-Lauraine et al. J Clin Oncol 2014 (AURELIA)

mustKnow.fact: Mirvetuximab soravtansine is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targeting folate receptor alpha (FR-alpha) conjugated to the tubulin inhibitor DM4; the phase III MIRASOL trial showed significant PFS and OS improvement (OS 16.5 vs 12.7 months; HR 0.67) in high FR-alpha-positive platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.

Platinum hypersensitivity reactions occur in up to 15% to 20% of patients receiving >=6 to 8 cycles of carboplatin; management comprises immediate infusion cessation, adrenaline/antihistamines, and implementation of a 12-step skin-testing-guided rapid desensitization protocol.
mustKnow.source: Castells et al. J Allergy Clin Immunol 2008

modules.name: Management of Surgical Complications: Ureteric Injury, Fistulae & Bowel Leak

topics.book: Berek & Hacker 7e Ch 25, DiSaia & Creasman 10e Ch 19

mustKnow.fact: The ureter is at greatest hazard for iatrogenic injury during radical gynecologic oncology surgery at four critical anatomical sites: at the pelvic brim where it crosses the common/external iliac bifurcation (infundibulopelvic ligament ligation), along the lateral pelvic sidewall, within the ureteric tunnel beneath the uterine artery, and at its insertion into the bladder trigone.

Management of distal third ureteric injury (within 4 to 5 cm of the bladder) is ureteroneocystostomy (ureteral reimplantation using Lich-Gregoir or Politano-Leadbetter anti-reflux technique) with a psoas hitch or Boari bladder flap to ensure a tension-free anastomosis over a double-J ureteral stent.

For mid-ureteric transection with adequate length and tension-free edges, primary end-to-end ureteroureterostomy over a double-J stent is performed with spatulated margins and interrupted 4-0/5-0 absorbable monofilament sutures (PDS/Monocryl).

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) following pelvic surgery typically presents 7 to 14 days post-operatively with continuous painless watery vaginal leakage; diagnostic confirmation is established via the classic double-dye test (oral phenazopyridine / Pyridium and intravesical methylene blue).

Surgical repair of a radiation-induced or complex recurrent vesicovaginal fistula requires complete scar excision, multilayer tension-free closure, and interposition of a well-vascularized tissue flap (Martius bulbocavernosus fat pad flap, gracilis flap, or omentum) with continuous bladder drainage for 14 to 21 days.

Early signs of gastrointestinal anastomotic leak or thermal bowel injury following cytoreduction appear between postoperative days 4 and 7, presenting with new-onset tachycardia, oliguria, unexplained metabolic acidosis, rising CRP, and feculent or purulent drain output.

Suspected peritonitis or septic shock from a postoperative bowel anastomotic leak mandates emergency exploratory laparotomy, extensive peritoneal lavage, exteriorization of the compromised bowel as a stoma (Hartmann's procedure for rectosigmoid leak), and delayed reconstruction after sepsis resolution.

Rectovaginal fistula following posterior pelvic exenteration or low anterior resection requires immediate proximal fecal diversion (loop colostomy or ileostomy); definitive fistula repair is deferred for a minimum of 3 to 6 months until radiation/surgical inflammation has subsided.

modules.name: Malignant Bowel Obstruction (MBO), Ascites & Palliative Care in Gynae-Oncology

mustKnow.fact: Malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) develops in 25% to 50% of patients with advanced, terminal epithelial ovarian cancer, resulting from diffuse peritoneal carcinomatosis, multi-segmental small bowel encasement, mesenteric foreshortening, and tumor infiltration of the myenteric autonomic plexus.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is the gold-standard diagnostic modality to evaluate MBO, differentiating a focal single-site mechanical obstruction (potentially amenable to surgical bypass or stenting) from multifocal, inoperable carcinomatosis.
mustKnow.source: Ripamonti et al. Ann Oncol 2012 (ESMO Guidelines)

mustKnow.fact: First-line pharmacological management of inoperable MBO utilizes a multimodal continuous subcutaneous or intravenous infusion combining octreotide (somatostatin analogue 300 to 600 mcg/day to reduce gastrointestinal secretions and luminal distension), haloperidol (antiemetic), and dexamethasone (6 to 8 mg/day to reduce peritumoral edema).
mustKnow.source: Mercadante et al. J Pain Symptom Manage 2000

mustKnow.fact: Prokinetic agents such as metoclopramide are strictly contraindicated in complete mechanical bowel obstruction due to the severe risk of excruciating colic pain, increased luminal pressure, and bowel wall perforation.

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) or venting gastrostomy tube placement is an effective minimally invasive palliative decompression procedure, eliminating persistent feculent vomiting and allowing discontinuation of painful nasogastric tubes in up to 90% of inoperable MBO patients.
mustKnow.source: Brooksbank et al. Support Care Cancer 2002

mustKnow.fact: Symptomatic recurrent malignant ascites is effectively palliated with indwelling tunneled peritoneal catheters (e.g., PleurX), which permit safe, intermittent, home-based drainage without requiring repeated hospital paracenteses.
mustKnow.source: Tapping et al. Eur J Surg Oncol 2012

mustKnow.fact: Catumaxomab (anti-EpCAM x anti-CD3 bispecific trifunctional antibody) administered as intraperitoneal infusions binds tumor EpCAM and T-cell CD3, destroying tumor cells and significantly extending puncture-free survival in malignant ascites from EpCAM-positive ovarian cancer.
mustKnow.source: Heiss et al. Int J Cancer 2010

mustKnow.fact: Neuropathic pelvic pain from lumbosacral plexus tumor infiltration is managed with adjuvant neuromodulators (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine) combined with scheduled opioid titration; superior hypogastric plexus neurolytic block achieves significant visceral pain reduction.
